content: Napalm refers to a category of flammable liquids, often jellied gasoline, used in warfare. The term napalm specifically denotes the thickening agent in these incendiary substances, which, when combined with gasoline, forms a sticky, incendiary gel. This innovation was developed during World War II by a team of Harvard chemists led by Louis Fieser. The name napalm is derived from the original ingredients, which were co-precipitated aluminum salts of naphthenic and palmitic acids. These compounds were added to flammable liquids to create a gel-like consistency. One of the primary issues with early incendiary fluids was their tendency to splash and drain too easily. The development of a gasoline gel significantly improved the range and effectiveness of flamethrowers. However, the initial formulations relied on natural rubber, which was both expensive and in high demand during the war. Napalm provided a more cost-effective alternative, addressing the limitations of rubber-based incendiaries. Modern napalm, known as napalm-B, is primarily composed of benzene and polystyrene. Napalm was first used in warfare on July 17, 1944, when American P-38 pilots dropped napalm incendiary bombs on a fuel depot near St. Lô, France. It was later employed extensively in the Pacific Theater during the Battle of Tinian by Marine aviators, although its use was initially complicated by issues with mixing, fusing, and release mechanisms. During World War II, the United States Army Air Forces (USAAF) used napalm in bombing campaigns over Japanese cities and in flamethrowers against German and Japanese-held positions. It was also used by the Greek National Army during the Greek Civil War, by United Nations forces in Korea, by France in the First Indochina War, and by the United States during the Vietnam War. Napalm's most well-known delivery method is through air-dropped incendiary bombs, but it has also been used in flamethrowers by combat infantry. Flamethrowers utilize a thinner version of the jellied gasoline to destroy gun emplacements, bunkers, and cave hideouts. During the Guadalcanal campaign, U.S. Marines found flamethrowers highly effective against Japanese positions. Napalm was not only a casualty weapon but also a psychological weapon, as Japanese soldiers were more likely to abandon positions when faced with napalm. Prisoners of war confirmed that they feared napalm more than any other weapon. Napalm causes death or injury through immolation and asphyxiation. Immolation leads to rapid loss of blood pressure, unconsciousness, and death. Third-degree burns caused by napalm are typically not painful at the time of injury because the intense heat destroys the skin's nerve endings. However, second-degree burns from smaller splashes of napalm are excruciatingly painful and often result in severe scarring, known as keloids, which can cause motor disturbances. Survivors of napalm attacks, such as Kim Phúc, have described the pain as unimaginable. Napalm burns at extremely high temperatures, reaching approximately 1,200°C (2,200°F), and its adhesive properties make it difficult to extinguish once it adheres to the skin. International law does not explicitly prohibit the use of napalm against military targets, but its use against civilian populations was banned under the United Nations Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in 1980. Protocol III of the CCW restricts the use of incendiary weapons, including napalm, but not all states have ratified this protocol. For example, the United States is a party to the CCW but did not sign Protocol III. Reports have suggested the use of napalm-like substances, such as Mark 77 firebombs, during the Iraq War. While these bombs do not contain traditional napalm (e.g., napalm-B), they produce similar incendiary effects and remain controversial. Napalm is typically a mixture of gasoline with thickening agents. Early thickening agents included soaps, aluminum, and magnesium palmitates and stearates. Depending on the amount of thickener added, the resulting viscosity can range from a syrupy liquid to a thick, rubbery gel. The material's hydrophobic properties make it resistant to water, complicating efforts to extinguish it. Thickened fuel also rebounds better from surfaces, making it more effective in urban environments. There are two main types of napalm: oil-based with aluminum soap thickener and oil-based with polymeric thickener (napalm-B). The U.S. military has used various thickeners, including M1, M2, and M4, each with specific chemical compositions and properties. Napalm-B, also known as super napalm, is a mixture of low-octane gasoline with benzene and polystyrene. It was widely used during the Vietnam War. Unlike conventional napalm, which burns for 15–30 seconds, napalm-B burns for up to 10 minutes, adheres better to surfaces, and offers improved destructive effects. It is also less prone to accidental ignition, reducing the risk of accidents caused by soldiers smoking. When burned, napalm-B produces a distinctive smell. In the early 1950s, Norway developed its own napalm formulation, known as Northick II, based on fatty acids from whale oil. This was due to the poor performance of American-produced thickening agents in cold climates. Some weapons utilize a pyrophoric variant, known as TPA (thickened pyrophoric agent), which is chemically triethylaluminum thickened with polyisobutylene. Napalm became widely recognized by the American public during the Vietnam War and has since been referenced in media and art. Its devastating effects and psychological impact have made it a symbol of the horrors of modern warfare.
